title: Song of Solomon 2:8–17
context: The WEB assigns 2:8–13 to the Beloved, who hears her beloved coming swiftly over the hills like a young deer and then recounts his invitation to rise and come away, because winter is past and spring has come with flowers, birdsong, ripening figs, and blossoming vines. Verses 14–15 are assigned to the Lover, who calls her his dove in the clefts of the rock and asks to see her face and hear her voice, followed by a request to catch the little foxes that spoil the vineyards; interpreters differ on who speaks verse 15 and on what the foxes represent. Verses 16–17 are assigned to the Beloved, who declares mutual belonging and asks him to return until the day is cool. Literal readers commonly see the joy, longing, and mutual commitment of love, along with the need to guard it from small threats. Figurative readers commonly hear God’s call to his people, or Christ’s call to the church, to come away into new life. Readers in both Arminian and Reformed traditions commonly hold both readings, and the passage is largely shared ground.

verses.text: The voice of my beloved! Behold, he comes, leaping on the mountains, skipping on the hills.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Beloved hearing the voice of her beloved as he comes leaping over the mountains. Love’s approach brings joy.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see eager anticipation of the beloved’s coming. Figurative readers commonly hear the coming of Christ to his people, swift and unhindered.

verses.text: My beloved is like a roe or a young deer. Behold, he stands behind our wall! He looks in at the windows. He glances through the lattice.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see him standing behind the wall and looking through the lattice, close yet still separated. Love seeks to be near.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the image of one who approaches and calls. Some figurative readers compare Christ standing at the door (compare Revelation 3:20), a reading held in both traditions.

verses.text: My beloved spoke, and said to me, “Rise up, my love, my beautiful one, and come away.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Beloved recalling his invitation to rise up and come away. Love calls for a free and glad response.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a tender summons from the beloved. Figurative readers commonly hear Christ’s call to his people, and both traditions commonly see the call as gracious.

verses.text: For behold, the winter is past. The rain is over and gone.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the announcement that winter is past and the rain is over. A new season of warmth and life has arrived for love.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the passing of winter as an image of renewal. Figurative readers commonly hear the end of a hard season and the arrival of grace, an image shared across both traditions.

verses.text: The flowers appear on the earth. The time of the singing has come, and the voice of the turtledove is heard in our land.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see flowers appearing, the time of singing, and the voice of the turtledove in the land. Creation itself celebrates.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the beauty of spring as a backdrop for love’s joy. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as delight in God’s good creation (compare Genesis 1:31).

verses.text: The fig tree ripens her green figs. The vines are in blossom. They give out their fragrance. Arise, my love, my beautiful one, and come away.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see ripening figs and fragrant vines, and the repeated call to arise and come away. The season invites a response.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the invitation framed by signs of new life. Figurative readers commonly hear the call to new life in Christ, held alongside a literal reading in both traditions.

verses.text: My dove in the clefts of the rock, in the hiding places of the mountainside, let me see your face. Let me hear your voice; for your voice is sweet and your face is lovely.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Lover calling the Beloved his dove in the clefts of the rock and asking to see her face and hear her voice. Love longs for open presence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a tender desire for the beloved’s company. Figurative readers commonly hear Christ’s delight in the prayers and praises of his people.

verses.text: Catch for us the foxes, the little foxes that plunder the vineyards; for our vineyards are in blossom.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see a call to catch the little foxes that spoil the blossoming vineyards. Small threats can harm a growing love.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the need to guard what is precious. Readers in both traditions commonly apply the image to small faults or dangers, though its exact meaning and speaker are debated.

verses.text: My beloved is mine, and I am his. He browses among the lilies.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Beloved declaring that her beloved is hers and she is his. Love is mutual belonging freely given.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see covenant belonging expressed in personal terms (compare Song of Solomon 6:3). Figurative readers commonly hear the mutual belonging of Christ and his church, a reading both traditions share.

verses.text: Until the day is cool, and the shadows flee away, turn, my beloved, and be like a roe or a young deer on the mountains of Bether.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Beloved asking him to return until the day is cool and the shadows flee away. Love waits and longs.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see longing for the beloved’s return. Figurative readers commonly hear the church awaiting Christ until the shadows of this age give way to full day.
